title: Harvest Home
carry_block_text: Take your sheaves to the wagon first.

puzzles.title: Which factor explains most?
puzzles.question: Use the season 3 plots in harvest_plots. Build three one-factor models of grain: by variety, by manure and by block, and run anovaTest() on each. Which factor explains the largest share of the variation in grain?
puzzles.starter_code:
season_3 <- harvest_plots %>%
  filter(season == 3)

buildModel(
  data = season_3,
  model_type = "linear_regression",
  formula = grain ~ ____
) %>%
  anovaTest()
puzzles.solution:
season_3 <- harvest_plots %>%
  filter(season == 3)

buildModel(
  data = season_3,
  model_type = "linear_regression",
  formula = grain ~ variety
) %>%
  anovaTest()

buildModel(
  data = season_3,
  model_type = "linear_regression",
  formula = grain ~ manure
) %>%
  anovaTest()

buildModel(
  data = season_3,
  model_type = "linear_regression",
  formula = grain ~ block
) %>%
  anovaTest()
puzzles.right_feedback: Right: its share is the biggest of the three.
puzzles.wrong_feedback: Not that one. Run all three models of grain and compare the share in each factor's own row.

puzzles.title: Read the interaction
puzzles.question: Use the season 3 plots in harvest_plots. Does the effect of manure on grain depend on the variety? Build one model of grain ~ variety * manure, run anovaTest(), and read the interaction row (it prints as variety:manure, or as manure:variety if you put manure first). What share of the variation in grain does the interaction explain?
puzzles.solution:
season_3 <- harvest_plots %>%
  filter(season == 3)

buildModel(
  data = season_3,
  model_type = "linear_regression",
  formula = grain ~ variety * manure
) %>%
  anovaTest()
puzzles.right_feedback: Right: that is the interaction's share, the part of the spread in grain that comes from manure working differently on different varieties.
puzzles.wrong_feedback: Not that one. Check the formula is grain ~ variety * manure, then read the share column in the variety:manure row (not the variety, manure or noise rows).

puzzles.title: The whole profile
puzzles.question: Use the season 3 plots in harvest_plots. The station's laboratory analysed the grain from every plot: grain_nitrogen, grain_phosphate and grain_potash (% of dry matter). Run permanovaTest(cbind(...) ~ variety * manure) on the grain's mineral profile, all three columns at once. Of the rows above total, which explains the largest share of the variation in the profile?
puzzles.starter_code:
season_3 <- harvest_plots %>%
  filter(season == 3)

season_3 %>%
  permanovaTest(____ ~ variety * manure)
puzzles.solution:
season_3 <- harvest_plots %>%
  filter(season == 3)

season_3 %>%
  permanovaTest(cbind(grain_nitrogen, grain_phosphate, grain_potash) ~ variety * manure)
puzzles.right_feedback: Right: that row holds the biggest share of the variation in the grain's mineral profile.
puzzles.wrong_feedback: Not that one. Check the left side is cbind(grain_nitrogen, grain_phosphate, grain_potash), then compare the share column across every row except total (p changes a little from run to run; the share does not).
